title: Open-access flags and the papers behind them
claim: A paper flagged open access by the major bibliographic indexes can be read in full at the location they give.
subject: Open-access metadata
not_linked: 010 — Rasmussen 2018 is the paper this entry's counterexample concerns, but 010's argument is about protein cross-seeding and does not depend on anything here. The connection is that this entry explains why 010's node is marked Unreadable.
stage_note: both nodes verified at source — they are the registry's own direct observations, so there is no citation chain outstanding. The hypothesis stays open: the rate is unmeasured, and a first sample of 600 records found no second case
plain_status: Three large indexes told us a paper was free to read. The file all three pointed at was a photograph of one figure, not the paper. How often that happens is not known — our own first count of 600 records found no other case like it.
summary: An index saying a paper is free is a claim about a file, not about a readable paper. One verified case where the file is an image; the rate is unmeasured, and our first sample of 600 found no second case.
lede: Researchers find papers through indexes that mark which are free to read. That mark is generated from the presence of a deposited file, not from any check that the file is the paper. This entry records one case where it was a photograph of a figure, and reports an attempt to measure how often that happens.
author: Priority Nexus LLC (AI-assisted research; the counterexample and the sample were produced directly from the named APIs on 12 October 2026)
conflicts: This entry arose from the registry's own work. The counterexample was found while trying to read a source for Entry 010, and the measurement below was run by the registry rather than taken from a published study.

preamble.title: Under Investigation — one case verified, the rate unknown

blocks.text: The counterexample below was checked directly and holds. The claim it bears on — that an open-access flag indicates a readable paper — is not thereby refuted in general, and the registry's own first attempt to measure the rate found no second case. Both results are recorded here.

Bibliographic indexes mark which papers are free to read. OpenAlex reports an `is_oa` field and an `oa_url`; Unpaywall reports `is_oa` and a list of `oa_locations`; Semantic Scholar reports `isOpenAccess` and an `openAccessPdf`. Tools, reference managers and literature searches pass these marks to researchers as an answer to "can I read this?"
The claim under examination is the one a reader takes from that mark: **that the location given will yield the full text.**

The marks are derived, not asserted by a person. An index records that a repository holds a file associated with a work, and sets the flag. Nothing in that chain opens the file to see whether it is the paper.
That a deposited file is the work. A repository record can hold a figure, a supplementary table, a poster, a cover sheet or an author's accepted manuscript, and the flag does not distinguish them.
What T1–T4 mean for this claim.

items.text: **T1** A flagged record is **observed** to point at something other than the paper.
**T2** The failure is shown to **repeat across indexes** for the same work, rather than being one index's error.
**T3** A **measured rate** is established on a defined sample of flagged records, by resolving each one.
**T4** The rate is **measured and reproduced** across indexes, repository types and fields, with the causes separated.

blocks.text: The claim is a T3/T4 matter. The evidence here reaches **T2**. One attempt at T3 is reported below and did not find a second case of the same kind.

nodes.heading: A flag that resolves to a photograph
nodes.citation: Rasmussen J, Krasemann S, Altmeppen H, et al. "Infectious prions do not induce Aβ deposition in an in vivo seeding model." *Acta Neuropathologica* 2018;135(6):965–967. [doi:10.1007/s00401-018-1848-5](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00401-018-1848-5)

details.label: What it shows
details.text: On 12 October 2026, three indexes reported this paper as open access. OpenAlex gave `oa_url`, Unpaywall gave it as the first of three `oa_locations`, and Semantic Scholar gave it as `openAccessPdf` with status GREEN. All three named the same file: `151136_figure.jpg` in the University of Zurich repository — an image of a single figure. The other two locations Unpaywall listed were the repository's own handle and DOI, which resolve to a record page rather than a text. The repository refuses automated requests; a reader attempting it by hand found nothing readable.

details.label: What it does not show
details.text: How often this happens. One work, checked once, on one day.

details.label: Files
details.text: The three API responses were read directly. The paper itself remains unread, which is why [[010-cross-seeding-as-true-templating|Entry 010]] marks it Unreadable.

nodes.heading: A first attempt at the rate, which found nothing
nodes.citation: The registry's own measurement, 12 October 2026: 600 consecutive OpenAlex records with `oa_status: green` — the class where the free copy sits in a repository rather than with the publisher — examined for what kind of file the `oa_url` points at.

details.label: What it shows
details.text: None of the 600 pointed at an image. About 11% ended in `.pdf`, roughly 74% had no file extension at all (repository landing pages), and the remainder were script or identifier endings. On this measure, the figure-image case is rare rather than typical.

details.label: What it does not show
details.text: Whether the 74% without an extension resolve to a readable paper. That is the question which matters most and this sample does not answer it: deciding it means fetching each location and inspecting what comes back, and many repositories refuse automated requests — the same obstacle that produced this entry.

details.label: Files
details.text: Query and counts reproducible from the OpenAlex API; the filter and sample size are stated above.

items.text: **Shown.** An open-access flag can point at a file that is not the paper, and the three largest indexes can carry the same wrong file at once, because they derive from overlapping sources rather than checking independently.
**Not shown.** That this is common. The registry's own first count found no second case in 600 records and is reported here whether or not it suits the entry.
**Unmeasured.** The rate at which a flagged location yields a readable full text, which is the number a researcher actually needs.

Take a defined sample of flagged open-access records — several hundred, stratified by index and repository platform — resolve each location, and classify what comes back: full text, landing page, fragment, nothing. That produces the rate. The obstacle is that repositories commonly block automated requests, so the sample has to be small enough to resolve by hand or run with repository cooperation.
Repeat the Rasmussen check across indexes for a sample of works to measure how often a wrong location is shared between them rather than unique to one.
**If the claim holds:** flagged locations resolve to full texts at a high rate, and cases like Rasmussen are isolated data errors.
**If it doesn't:** a measurable share of "free to read" marks do not yield a readable paper, and the mark means something weaker than every tool presenting it implies.

blocks.text: An index flag can point at a figure rather than a paper → shown, verified across three indexes. That this is common → not shown; our own 600-record sample found no second case. The rate at which a flag yields a readable paper → unmeasured.

This entry has an unusual conflict and it is stated in the properties above: it came out of the registry's own work rather than from the literature, and the measurement in the second node was run by the registry, not taken from a published study. It has not been peer reviewed, and the 600-record sample is a first count rather than a designed study. The counterexample is reproducible from the three APIs named; the sample is reproducible from the OpenAlex filter named.
